detail.longDescription: AGENTS.md vs CLAUDE.md vs Skills vs MCP: What Actually Belongs Where? I use multiple AI coding agents in my development workflow. Claude Code for some tasks. Codex for others. Cursor when I want to work directly inside the editor. At first, my approach was simple: Give each AI tool enough instructions to understand the project. That worked. Until it didn't. Soon, the repository started accumulating instructions everywhere: CLAUDE.md AGENTS.md README.md architecture docs feature plans skills MCP configurations random prompts And many of them were saying almost the same thing. Even worse, I was starting to mix project rules , architecture , feature requirements , and agent workflows into the same files. The problem wasn't that the AI needed more context. The problem was that I had no clear architecture for that context. So I changed the way I organize AI instructions in my projects. This is the structure I'm using in 2026. The Problem: Every AI Agent Wants Context Imagine you're working on a production application with: Next.js TypeScript React a backend API authentication permissions tests CI/CD established architecture You ask an AI agent: Add filtering to the users page. That sounds simple. But the agent needs to know much more. Should it create a new component? Is there already a shared filter component? Where does data fetching happen? Are filters stored in URL parameters? Which naming conventions does the project use? Should the agent add tests? Can it modify the API? Without that context, the AI starts making assumptions. And assumptions are where AI-generated code becomes expensive. My First Solution Was a Giant Instruction File Like many developers, I started adding everything to one file. Something like: CLAUDE.md Project architecture Coding conventions Folder structure Testing rules API conventions React conventions TypeScript conventions Git rules UI rules Feature notes Deployment notes Eventually it became hundreds of lines. Technically, the agent had more information. Practically, I had created another problem: Every task was receiving context that had nothing to do with that task. A UI change didn't need deployment instructions. A backend bug didn't need the entire React architecture. A database migration didn't need animation guidelines. More context is not automatically better context. The Mental Model I Use Now I stopped treating AI context as one big instruction file. Instead, I separate it by responsibility . ContextResponsibilityExample AGENTS.md Repository-wide agent instructionsconventions, commands, boundaries CLAUDE.md Claude-specific guidanceClaude-specific behavior or workflow intent.md What a particular change should accomplishrequirements, constraints, acceptance criteriaArchitecture docsHow the system worksauth flow, modules, data flowSkillsHow to perform repeatable taskscode review, testing, migrationsMCPAccess to external systemsGitHub, documentation, databases, tools The important idea is: These files don't compete with each other. They solve different context problems. Let's break that down. 1. AGENTS.md : How Agents Should Work in This Repository I treat AGENTS.md as the repository-level contract for coding agents. It contains things that should remain true regardless of the feature being implemented. For example: # Project Next.js 16 application using TypeScript and App Router. ## Commands npm run dev npm run test npm run lint npm run build ## Architecture - Server Components by default. - Use Client Components only when browser APIs or interactivity require them. - API access goes through `src/lib/api`. - Shared UI components live under `src/components/ui`. ## TypeScript - Do not use `any`. - Prefer inferred types when the source already provides the type. - Derive API types from schemas where possible. ## Implementation Rules - Search for an existing abstraction before creating one. - Do not introduce a new dependency without justification. - Keep changes scoped to the requested feature. - Run relevant tests after implementation. Notice what isn't there: "Add the customer filter requested in ticket # 124." That's not a repository rule. That's feature intent. This distinction matters. 2. CLAUDE.md : Claude-Specific Context If I'm using Claude Code, there may still be instructions that only make sense for Claude. That's where CLAUDE.md becomes useful. For example: # Claude Code Instructions Before implementing a non-trivial feature: 1. Investigate the existing implementation. 2. Identify reusable patterns. 3. Explain the proposed change. 4. Implement only after the approach is clear. When investigating bugs: - Trace the full execution path. - Identify the root cause before patching symptoms. - Check whether similar code exists elsewhere. The distinction I try to maintain is: AGENTS.md ↓ How agents work in this repository CLAUDE.md ↓ Additional instructions specifically useful to Claude That reduces duplication. If a rule should apply to every coding agent, I don't want three copies of it. 3. intent.md : What Are We Actually Trying to Change? This is one of the most useful additions to my workflow. Repository instructions explain how to work . Architecture documentation explains how the system works . But neither explains: Why are we making this particular change? That's where feature intent comes in. For example: # Intent Users need to filter the orders table by delivery status. ## Expected behavior The user can select: - Pending - In Progress - Completed - Cancelled The selected filters must persist in the URL. ## Constraints - Use the existing table filtering architecture. - Do not introduce a second filtering system. - Backend endpoints must remain unchanged. ## Acceptance criteria - Multiple statuses can be selected. - Refreshing the page preserves filters. - Clearing filters restores the complete list. Now the coding agent has something extremely valuable: a definition of success. Without intent, AI agents often optimize for: "Make the requested code change." With intent, they can optimize for: "Produce the expected behavior while respecting the system's constraints." That's a much better target. 4. Architecture Docs: Explain the System, Not the Task Some information doesn't belong in either AGENTS.md or intent.md . For example: How authentication works How multi-tenancy works How permissions are calculated How the API client works How background jobs are processed Those are architecture concerns. So I keep them separately: docs/ ├── architecture.md ├── authentication.md ├── permissions.md ├── api.md └── deployment.md Then agents can inspect the relevant documentation when needed. Instead of putting 500 lines of architecture into every prompt, I can say: Review the authentication architecture before changing the login flow. The context becomes discoverable instead of permanently injected . That's a major difference. 5. Skills: Teach the Agent Repeatable Workflows Some instructions aren't really project rules. They're procedures. For example: How should you review a pull request? How should you investigate a regression? How should you create a database migration? How should you perform a UI parity review? These are repeatable workflows. That's how I think about agent skills. A simplified structure might look like: .claude/ └── skills/ ├── code-review/ │ └── SKILL.md ├── regression-analysis/ │ └── SKILL.md └── frontend-review/ └── SKILL.md A code-review skill might contain: # Code Review When reviewing a change: 1. Understand the requested behavior. 2. Inspect the diff. 3. Trace affected execution paths. 4. Look for regressions. 5. Check existing project patterns. 6. Verify tests. 7. Report findings by severity. Do not modify code unless explicitly requested. Now I don't need to rewrite that workflow every time. 6. MCP: Give Agents Capabilities, Not More Instructions MCP solves a different problem. Sometimes the agent doesn't lack instructions. It lacks access . For example, it may need information from: GitHub documentation issue trackers databases browser tools design systems internal services That's where MCP fits into my mental model. Instructions → Tell the agent how to behave Documentation → Tell the agent how the system works Intent → Tell the agent what needs to change Skills → Tell the agent how to perform a workflow MCP → Give the agent access to external capabilities/context Mixing these concepts together is where AI setups become unnecessarily complicated. My Repository Structure A simplified version of the setup looks like this: my-project/ │ ├── AGENTS.md ├── CLAUDE.md │ ├── intent/ │ ├── feature-a.md │ └── feature-b.md │ ├── docs/ │ ├── architecture.md │ ├── authentication.md │ └── api.md │ ├── .claude/ │ └── skills/ │ ├── code-review/ │ └── regression-analysis/ │ └── src/ Each layer answers a different question. QuestionWhere I put itHow should an agent work here? AGENTS.md Does Claude need special guidance? CLAUDE.md What are we trying to accomplish? intent.md How does this system work? docs/ How should a repeatable task be performed?SkillsDoes the agent need external access?MCP This separation makes the repository much easier for both humans and agents to reason about. What I Stopped Doing There are several patterns I've gradually removed from my workflow. ❌ One 1,000-line AI instruction file Large instruction files become dumping grounds. I prefer smaller pieces of context with clear ownership. ❌ Repeating the same rules for every agent If Claude, Codex, and another agent all need the same repository rule, maintaining three versions creates drift. ❌ Putting feature requirements into permanent instructions A temporary feature requirement should not become a permanent repository rule. ❌ Explaining the entire architecture in every prompt Let the agent investigate relevant documentation and code. ❌ Asking the agent to immediately code This one is important. For non-trivial work, my workflow increasingly looks like: Understand ↓ Investigate ↓ Plan ↓ Implement ↓ Verify Not: Prompt ↓ Generate code ↓ Hope A Realistic Workflow Suppose I receive this requirement: Add an Edit Vehicle action to the trip card. Instead of giving the AI a massive prompt describing the entire application, I can provide the feature intent: # Intent Add an explicit Edit Vehicle action to trip cards. ## Requirements - Respect the existing vehicle-edit permission. - Reuse the existing vehicle editing flow. - Do not create a new modal if an existing one can be reused. - Preserve the current trip-card layout. ## Verification - Authorized users can edit. - Unauthorized users do not see the action. - Existing trip actions continue working. Then my prompt becomes much smaller: Review the intent for this feature. Investigate the existing trip card, vehicle editing flow, and permission implementation. Before changing code, explain which existing components and patterns should be reused. Then implement the smallest change that satisfies the intent and run the relevant tests. Notice what's missing. I don't explain the folder structure. I don't explain TypeScript conventions. I don't explain how permissions generally work. I don't explain testing commands. The repository already knows those things. Context Engineering > Prompt Engineering This changed how I think about AI-assisted development. Early AI coding workflows focused heavily on: "How do I write the perfect prompt?" I increasingly think the more important question is: "What information should the agent have access to at this moment?" Consider these two approaches. Approach A [2,000-word prompt containing everything] Please implement this feature. Approach B Repository rules + Relevant architecture + Feature intent + Existing code + Task-specific workflow The second approach usually produces a better environment for reasoning. The prompt itself can become surprisingly small. The Goal Isn't Maximum Context This is probably the biggest lesson I've learned. AI agents don't necessarily need more context . They need: the right context, at the right time, with a clear responsibility. Too little context produces assumptions. Too much irrelevant context produces noise. Good context engineering sits between those extremes. One Repository, Multiple Agents The biggest benefit of this architecture is that I'm no longer designing my repository around one AI tool. The repository itself contains the knowledge. ┌─────────────┐ │ AGENTS.md │ └──────┬──────┘ │ Repository conventions │ ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐ │ │ │ ▼ ▼ ▼ Claude Code Codex Cursor │ │ │ └────────────────┼────────────────┘ │ Project knowledge │ ┌───────────────┼───────────────┐ ▼ ▼ ▼ Intent Architecture Skills Different agents can still have tool-specific configuration. But the core project knowledge isn't trapped inside one AI ecosystem. And that's increasingly important. My Rule of Thumb When I'm about to add something to my AI setup, I ask one question: What kind of context is this? If it's a permanent repository rule: → AGENTS.md If it's Claude-specific: → CLAUDE.md If it describes what a change should accomplish: → intent.md If it explains the system: → architecture documentation If it's a repeatable procedure: → skill If it provides access to an external system: → MCP That simple classification has prevented a lot of instruction-file chaos. Final Thought AI coding agents are becoming better at writing code. But writing code is increasingly not the difficult part. The difficult part is giving the agent enough understanding to make the right change inside an existing system . That's why I think the next stage of AI-assisted development isn't going to be about increasingly elaborate prompts. It's going to be about context architecture . Structure the repository so that both humans and AI agents can answer: How should I work here? How does this system work? What are we trying to change? What constraints must I respect? How do I verify that I'm done? When those answers are clear, the specific coding agent becomes much less important. And that's exactly what I want. What's Your Setup? I'm curious how other developers are handling this now that many of us use more than one coding agent. Are you keeping everything in AGENTS.md ? Do you maintain separate CLAUDE.md instructions? Are you using skills or MCP? Or has your repository also started accumulating AI instruction files everywhere? Share your setup in the comments. If you're interested, I'll write a follow-up showing the actual AGENTS.md structure and AI workflow I use for a production Next.js + TypeScript project . # ai # programming # productivity # claudecode # software # coding # development # engineering # inclusive # community I Stopped Writing Separate Instructions for Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor - Here's My 2026 Setup
